scenes.narration: Open Med Check. A prescribing check that reads the doctor's note, powered by Gemma 4, and built to run on a hospital's own hardware.

Emergency doctors sign orders under time pressure. Most prescribing checks look at drug pairs and coded data; the ones we looked at don't read the free-text note. Clinicians override between half and over ninety percent of medication alerts, and the W H O estimates that medication errors cost forty-two billion dollars a year.

Take this synthetic patient: chest pain, on daily aspirin. The note says: suspected acute coronary syndrome. The order is dexketoprofen, an anti-inflammatory. The coded record has no diagnosis yet, so the rules alone find no issue.
Here is the app. We open bed three, and fill in the test prescription.
Gemma reads the note and quotes it. The rules decide from those quotes: blocked, with the doctor's own words as the evidence, and an alternative the rules have already re-checked.
One click re-checks paracetamol: no issue found by these checks. The prescriber still decides.

Gemma reads, and the rules decide. Every quote is checked word for word against the note. The model can raise a verdict, but never lower it. And if the model fails, the card falls back to the rules and says so: a clean result becomes a warning that the note was not checked.

On seventy-six synthetic cases we wrote ourselves, a development set and not a clinical validation, the rules alone gave the expected result seventy-two percent of the time. With Gemma reading the note: ninety-seven percent, and no false alarm on the thirty-four cases that should stay silent.

Because Gemma 4 is open-weight, it can run on a hospital's own G P U, so the note never has to leave the building. We think the buyer is the hospital's medication-safety team: the engine stays open source, and they would pay for a maintained rule table, integration, and support. That is still a hypothesis we haven't tested with buyers.
Open Med Check. Open source, on GitHub. Not for clinical use: synthetic patients only. Not a medical device.
